text: This lesson ties the whole cluster together into one practical rule: pick the loosest isolation level that still prevents the specific anomalies your business logic actually cares about. Every level stricter than that is pure cost -- more blocking, for a guarantee nothing in your code is actually relying on.

For almost everything, start at READ COMMITTED -- the default -- or RCSI if reader-writer blocking is a measurable problem. Only reach for REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE when you can name the specific anomaly that would otherwise be a real bug. And for reporting or read-heavy work that shouldn't block writers, SNAPSHOT or RCSI are usually the strongest fit.

RCSI is almost always the first move if READ COMMITTED's default blocking is causing real problems -- it keeps the exact same guarantees, served with far less blocking, and needs no code changes at all.

Moving stricter should always be for a reason you can state out loud. REPEATABLE READ, because a nonrepeatable read would genuinely break this specific piece of logic. SERIALIZABLE, because a phantom row would break an exact reconciliation. Never reach for either one just to feel safe -- name the anomaly first.

Here's a worked example: a nightly batch job that counts open orders at the start of a run and again at the end, and the counts must match exactly, even while other sessions are actively inserting and cancelling orders. A phantom row would break that reconciliation -- so this one specific piece of the job genuinely needs SERIALIZABLE, while everything else it touches stays at READ COMMITTED or RCSI.

That closes out this isolation-levels cluster -- three anomalies, six levels, and now a framework for choosing between them. Next, we go back to concurrency and blocking with all of that in hand. See you there.
